overview: The Sámi are an Indigenous people whose homeland, Sápmi, crosses northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula. They speak several related languages and have pursued varied livelihoods, including fishing, hunting, handicrafts and reindeer husbandry. No single occupation or modern national border defines the whole people.

periods.title: A northern traveler describes Sámi livelihoods
periods.summary: Ottarr’s report to the English court describes domestic reindeer and tribute in hides, feathers, tusks and other materials. It is an outside account, not a Sámi description of their own institutions.

periods.title: Herding and seasonal camps develop
periods.summary: In areas with intensive reindeer husbandry, milking, transport and repeated movement between seasonal camps organized household work. This regional pattern did not replace fishing and other livelihoods throughout Sápmi.

periods.title: National borders interrupt migration routes
periods.summary: Reindeer movements across the Norway-Finland border were prohibited in 1852. Closure of the Finland-Sweden border to such movement followed in 1889, disrupting established grazing arrangements.

periods.title: School policy meets organized opposition
periods.summary: Sweden’s 1913 reform separated children of mobile herders from other pupils. At the 1918 Sámi meeting in Östersund, participants demanded better schooling and an end to inadequate school huts.

periods.title: A Sámi museum opens at Inari
periods.summary: Founded through Sámi organization, the museum now known as Siida opened its outdoor displays in 1963. Preserving buildings and objects became one means of protecting cultural knowledge.

periods.title: Representative institutions begin work
periods.summary: Sámi parliaments began operating in Norway in 1989, Sweden in 1993 and Finland in 1996. Their responsibilities differ under each country’s institutions and laws.

items.text: Fishing in seas, lakes and rivers supported many Sámi communities, while organized hunting required knowledge of animal routes and behavior. Surviving pit systems record collective work in hunting landscapes. Reindeer herding became highly visible, but treating every Sámi family as a herd-owning household obscures this wider economic history.

A seasonal herding camp needed pasture, fresh water, fuel, building materials and suitable dry ground. Cold springs or ground suitable for storage helped keep milk. Choosing a location therefore involved practical knowledge of several resources at once, rather than simply following animals without a planned pattern of return.

Reindeer milking was labor-intensive and could involve the whole family. Herders moved among different milking grounds during summer; mountain routes also used snow patches where animals found relief from insects and heat. These are descriptions of particular herding systems, not evidence that the same schedule applied to coastal fishers or every Sámi region.

Sámi languages are related but distinct. In Finland, Northern Sámi, Inari Sámi and Skolt Sámi each have their own communities and histories. Language is part of work and the transmission of skills, as well as schooling and literature. Calling all of these languages a single uniform tongue would hide that diversity.

Duodji joins making, use and cultural knowledge. Materials include birch bark, roots, hide, sinew and reindeer antler. Portable containers, knives and clothing were shaped for particular tasks and for movement where required. Craftsmanship also continues as art and a livelihood; a museum object is one moment in an evolving practice.

The náhppi, a vessel for milking reindeer, illustrates how a household object’s form addressed a practical problem: limiting spillage. Containers could be carved from birch burls or root growths. Such work required understanding the material as well as the task. This is a documented object type, not a claim about an excavated specimen’s date.

Tirro Farm at Siida represents nineteenth-century Sámi life in permanent houses. Its place among movable tents, shelters and storage buildings makes an important distinction visible: Sámi architecture included several forms, suited to different livelihoods. The museum setting is a curated presentation, rather than an untouched nineteenth-century village.

Siida also preserves Mirhamintupa, a courthouse moved from the Inari-Kittilä border. Names and inscriptions left by people awaiting sentences survive on its walls. The building offers a different kind of evidence from hunting tools: a physical trace of encounters with judicial authority, preserved in a structure relocated for interpretation.

Medieval sagas and chronicles describe Sámi people through their authors’ interests. Ottarr’s account, for example, connects northern resources with tribute. Such texts can reveal trade and relations of power, but they should not be read as a complete census, a neutral ethnography or proof that every named northern group was identical.

Border closures divided grazing systems that had crossed what became national frontiers. Some herders moved from Kautokeino to Karesuando after 1852 and continued using Finnish winter pasture as Swedish subjects, until the later closure blocked that route too. State lines changed practical access to land without making Sámi relationships stop at those lines.

The Swedish school system distinguished children by their families’ livelihoods and offered mobile herders’ children inferior conditions. Sámi delegates challenged both the physical accommodation and the limited educational expectations in 1918. Their demands show parents and organizers seeking the knowledge children needed for a changing society, while resisting policies imposed upon them.

Elsa Laula Renberg helped bring together the cross-border Sámi congress held in Trondheim on 6 February 1917. Organizing across state boundaries became an enduring part of Sámi public life. The event is commemorated by Sámi National Day, linking contemporary civic expression with an earlier achievement in collective representation.

Finland’s Sámi Parliament works on language, culture and Indigenous status, while the Skolt Sámi also have a separate decision-making body. Norway and Sweden have their own Sámi parliaments. These institutions should be understood in their particular settings; they are not a single sovereign state governing all of Sápmi.

ending.text: The Sámi continue as a people across several states, maintaining languages, livelihoods, cultural institutions and political representation. Borders and state policies restricted land use and shaped community life, but there was no single event in which a unified Sámi kingdom fell. The imported map intervals describe coverage, not the people’s lifetime.
